title: The Fathers on Galatians
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Neither Moses nor any prophet died for the world; Christ did.
comments.comment: Galatians 1:4 shows that neither Moses died for the sake of the world, nor any other of the prophets. Therefore one must not be defeated by the one who did not save, but by the one who died for us.
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain words why Christ's giving himself matters: no one else died for the world.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Whoever does not offer himself to Christ, who gave himself to deliver us from the present evil age, is owned by that age and ruled by sin by his own willing.
comments.comment: But every sinner is tyrannized by the 'ruler of this age,' since every sinner is owned by the present evil age, not offering himself to him who 'gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age' (Galatians 1:4) — and he 'delivers' 'according to the will of our God and Father,' (Galatians 1:4) according to what is said in Galatians. And he who is tyrannized by this ruler of the age is ruled by sin by the voluntariness of his sinning.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul uses "age" for the wicked system of human error and sin, and "world" for the created order.
comments.comment: … "World" is used in two ways: the created order, and the wicked system of human beings. Here [in Ephesians 2:2, "the age of this world"] Paul divided the two realities, calling human wickedness and sin "age," and the constitution of the universe "world," just as he also says in Galatians: "to rescue us from the present evil age" (Galatians 1:4). He means this present age. So he named the common human rebellion and error "age," of which those who now believe in Christ were once a part.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by "the present evil age".
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Some Jewish believers talked the Galatians into keeping the law, which turned the gospel they and the apostles shared into a different one.
comments.comment:
Regarding the proclamation to the nations, having received it, some from the circumcised community, departing, were persuading the nations to Judaize; and first concerning this it appears that a search has happened in Antioch, that the apostles wrote not to be under the law, but to abstain from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication; for so it seemed to the Holy Spirit. And this disease prevailed among the Galatians, in agreement with those having willed to Judaize. And they were persuaded by those perverting the truth, saying, that the rest of the apostles do not forbid those willing to keep the law. …

Galatians 1:6–7 He says, 'Into a different gospel, which is not another gospel'; for your gospel and that of the apostles is willed to be outside of you by the law.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Since the Holy Spirit does not change his mind, any changed preaching is to be set aside, and one who still pleased men would not serve Christ.
comments.comment:
Galatians 1:8–10 'Let him be an angel, why then also we?; when we were proclaiming, by the power of the Holy Spirit we proclaimed'; and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. If therefore we say other things, we have abandoned the things of the Spirit. Let the preacher be an anathema, then, setting aside the proclamation. From what you received. 'I did not proclaim, he says, but you did not receive, but also I proclaimed, and you received.' 'Neither do I repent having proclaimed, and you have observed what you received.' 'For now am I persuading men or God?; or am I seeking to please men?; if I were still pleasing men, I would not have been a slave of Christ.'

Intending to remind them of his own gospel, he anticipates the objection so that they may not think that he heals by submitting; for he strikes by rebuking. Having said 'if still', he showed that he once pleased men. What, indeed, pleased him? From whom the faithful ones to Damascus received letters to afflict. If therefore, he says, he were still pleasing the Jews, he would not have believed in Christ.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's gospel came by revelation from the one who became man, so what he preaches cannot fail to be true.
comments.comment: He [Paul] says that he delivered to them, not something that had simply come into his mind and been accepted without testing, but the gospel that he received, since the one who became man for our sake put the knowledge of it into him. For the same apostle says again of the gospel, “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12). If, then, the one who hands it on is taught by God, how can what he preaches not be true: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), that is, both the Old and the New?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul left the law not out of hatred, since he had defended it, but because he found the perfect, and he means no slander of the apostles.
comments.comment:
Galatians 1:13 'What need is there of a turning in Judaism, but that he might show that he does not serve beforehand but in truth'; for not having hated the law did he run away from grace—for he was persecuting it—but having found the perfect, he departed from the law. Now he shows that he has more than that concerning Peter; for those did not zeal for the sake of Judaism, disobeying Christianity, as I do. Do not therefore think that having hated the law I came into grace—for I was defending the law—but I found the perfect, and I do not put the law on a level with perfect grace.

Galatians 1:16 He says this not slandering the apostles, but that I did not run in step with fleshly flesh.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Having received revelation from God, Paul had no need of human teaching, so he did not consult flesh and blood.
comments.comment: “But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son in me, that I might proclaim him among the nations, immediately I did not consult with flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me.” (Galatians 1:15–17) For the one who has once obtained the initiation and revelation from God did not need the tutoring that comes from humans.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul did not go to Jerusalem or consult anyone after his call.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: James is called the Lord's brother for his character more than blood.
comments.comment: This James is the one whom Paul, a true disciple of Jesus, says he saw, calling him “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), not so much because of kinship by blood or their shared upbringing as because of his character and his teaching.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Paul calls James "the Lord's brother".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter, afraid of the Jews, withdrew from the Gentiles, and the pillars kept Jewish customs while Paul and Barnabas went to the Gentiles.
comments.comment: In the Epistle to the Galatians, too, Paul shows that Peter, still afraid of the Jews, stopped eating with the Gentiles, and when James came to him “he separated himself” from the Gentiles, “fearing those of the circumcision”; and the rest of the Jews and Barnabas did the same as he did (Galatians 2:12–13). And it was consistent that those who had been sent to the circumcision should not depart from the Jewish customs, when “those who were reputed to be pillars gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship,” and went off themselves “to the circumcision,” so that those two might preach to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul blamed Peter not for yielding to the weak but for drawing many Gentile believers toward living by the law.
comments.comment: … For even if Paul blamed Peter for living like a Jew because of those who had come to Antioch from James (Galatians 2:11–14), he did not blame him for stooping to the weakness of those of the circumcision and abstaining from foods. He blamed him because, by the weight of his own standing, he was drawing the many believers from the nations into thinking that they had to live according to the law, and Paul’s preaching was in danger of coming to nothing; for he was the teacher of the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains exactly what Paul blamed Peter for at Antioch.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Works of the law bring toil while faith brings ease and righteousness, so one should let the law go and be content with grace.
comments.comment: Galatians 2:16 For if no one is justified from works, which bring toil, but from faith, where both the ease and the righteousness are great, how is it not necessary, he says, to let the law go and be content with grace? He says one is not justified from works of the law, not from the commandments; for the commandment justifies when it is heard, but the work was the thing hard to accomplish.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: To die to the law is to follow the law of faith and no longer work what was marked out for the ancients in shadow and types, so as to live to God.
comments.comment:
“For through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:19–20)

What, then, does the inspired Paul mean here? A law was set by God through the voice of the prophets, and it was this: “The righteous shall live by faith.” (Habakkuk 2:4) A law was also set through Moses. So having followed the law of faith, he says, I died to the law through Moses — no longer working the things marked out for the ancients as in shadow and types. For that is what it means to die to the Mosaic law: that we may live to God, clinging to faith in Christ (Romans 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Paul died to the law in order to live to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: To die to the world and to sins, and to live holy for God, is to undergo the dying of Christ and live the life that is in him.
comments.comment: [The dying of Christ is this:] To have died to the world and to sins, and to live out a life that is sacred and holy and as dear to God as possible. Paul again took great pride in this, when he said: ‘For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me’ (Galatians 2:19–20). This, I think, is what it means to have died to the world and to have undergone the dying of Christ, and in turn to live out the life that is in him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The law concerns bodily observances for people on earth, but Christ lives in Paul and is in heaven, so Paul is not under the law.
comments.comment: The law of bodily things has the work and the enjoyment: eat this and do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, circumcision (Gal 2:19–21). Grace does not wish to be pleased in you through these things. I have been crucified with these, he says. What need have I of law? I live no longer, but Christ lives in me. What I was living to myself, I was under law. But since Christ lives in me—he who is no longer under law but is in the heavens at the right hand of the Father—he does not negate the one living in me. But what I now live in the flesh, I live in faith. For I believe into the Son of God. And if the Son of God, whom I believe, is at the right hand of the Father, I live as a citizen in the heavens; but the law had the observances for those on earth. Therefore, I am not subject to law.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ lives in those who work according to him, and those who call themselves Christians but do not do so do not have him living in them.
comments.comment: … so that each one says: 'But Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20). Such a person is in Christ and has Christ in himself, living and working. But when someone perceives him not as living nor working, he forgets him as if dead; for Christ does not live in all, but in those working according to him. And those who consider themselves to be Christians, but do not work according to Christ, do not have him living in them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word wills that Christ, not our own soul, move our bodies, and we become his members when we move everything according to his word.
comments.comment: Human bodies are instruments of the soul; and when the soul rules, the body serves and is used for whatever the soul wishes. But the Word especially wills that our bodies no longer be energized by our own soul but by Christ himself; therefore Paul says: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). They become members of Christ, then, when we move everything according to his word.
comments.selected_reason: Makes clear in everyday terms what "Christ lives in me" means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law, though God's, gave no supply of the Spirit and no power to work wonders, but faith in Christ gives both.
comments.comment: “He who supplies the Spirit to you and works powers…” (Galatians 3:5) The law through Moses, though it is God’s law and “spoken through angels,” (Hebrews 2:2) (Galatians 3:19) does not have the supply of the Holy Spirit, nor did it procure for anyone the power to work wonders. But through faith in Christ we gain both. How then is faith in him not better, if it has abolished the old law?
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's question about who supplies the Spirit and works powers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Abraham's children are not those descended from him in the flesh but those of faith.
comments.comment: Indeed, the Savior himself, most strongly rebuking those who claim to have Abraham as a father according to the flesh, said: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham' (John 8:39). By this understanding, 'the vessel of election,' the apostle Paul writes to the Church, clarifying how the holy patriarch is a father of the nations, asserting: 'As many as are of faith, these are sons of Abraham, being blessed with him' (Galatians 3:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham was justified by believing God, and the nations are justified likewise by following in his steps and believing in Christ.
comments.comment: For it is written that “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto righteousness,” (Genesis 15:6) and it was said to him that “in you all the tribes of the earth will be blessed.” (Genesis 12:3) And Paul made it clear for us, saying: “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through law, but through righteousness of faith,” (Romans 4:13) and again: “so that those from faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.” (Galatians 3:9) … For blessed Abraham was justified having believed toward God; so also the nations would be justified in him, having followed in his steps and believing in God—that is, in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how those of faith are blessed with Abraham.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The Law justifies least of all since it condemns, and Paul shows its weakness by saying that the righteous live from faith.
comments.comment: For if what is under sin is still a slave, and the Law justifies least of all — it condemns rather, and writes down those who transgress — how would it not be clear to everyone that all justification is in Christ, and the perfecting in the Spirit through sanctification, through him and in him? … And he [Paul] writes down the uselessness and weakness of the old Law in this, saying, 'That no one is justified in the Law before God is clear, because the righteous shall live from faith. And the Law is not from faith, but the one who has done them shall live in them.' (Galatians 3:11–12) So in Christ we are justified through faith, and we have been redeemed from the intelligible slavery.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says no one is justified by the Law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The law curses the sinner, yet Christ, who knew no sin, took the curse on himself and died for all, to loose everyone's disobedience.
comments.comment: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” (Deuteronomy 21:23) (Galatians 3:13) While the letter of the law declares cursed the one in transgression and sins, the One who did not know sin — that is, Christ — was brought under the curse, enduring an unjust sentence and suffering what befits those under a curse, so that the One worth all, dying for all, might loose the charges of everyone’s disobedience and buy what is under heaven with his own blood.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how the sinless Christ became a curse for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ's death saves the world: hanging on the tree he became a curse to loose the world's sin, so that the nations might be justified and receive the Spirit.
comments.comment: Look here too: Christ’s death has become saving for the world. For he became a curse for us, enduring a cross and hanging on a tree, so that he might loose the world’s sin, “so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus” — that is, so that the nations might be justified through faith according to the promise given to Abraham, “so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Christ's becoming a curse accomplished for the nations.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The name of the curse signifies the cross, and Christ became dead to make the dead alive and poor to make others rich.
comments.comment: “so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations”—and a blessing that is productive is not, in reality, a curse. The productive things of the good are good. The productive things of those pleasing to God are themselves pleasing to God. And the name of the curse signifies the cross, just as the apostle himself, having written this voice, demonstrated. He said: “For it is written: cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree” (Gal 3:13), and just as he became dead, in order to show and make the dead alive, and he became dead in death, in order to destroy death and to set free those held by it; so also he became poor, in order that through his poverty they might become rich for whom the poor became poor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the law came four hundred and thirty years after the promise, the promise concerns faith, or Abraham and the holy people before the law would be shut out of the blessing.
comments.comment: But since you confess that transgressors under the law are not heirs of the blessing, because for such people the law produces wrath (Romans 4:15), it is clear that the promise concerns faith, not circumcision. The promise would be destroyed if no one were righteous apart from the law. For the law, introduced four hundred and thirty years after the promise (Galatians 3:17), would show Abraham himself, Isaac, Jacob, and all the holy people in between excluded from a blessing which could not have been conferred on anyone without the law.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Before the law the mind and flesh served sin, and when the law was given it disciplined the mind though it could not free the flesh.
comments.comment: … How then was it added because of transgressions, he says? In a short word, it is this: before the law, the mind of men, along with the flesh, served sin and cherished evil; when the law was given, the mind was disciplined, but the flesh was still held captive. Therefore, since the one ignorant of sin, knowing it was sin, treated impiety as piety and attended to it more eagerly, but the one having known that it is evil, this one indeed gains the conscience that it transgresses, and desires to obey God. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The Law came in so that the trespass would increase and show our need of forgiveness, and Paul answers anyone who thinks the Law set aside the promise.
comments.comment: So the Law came in besides, so that the trespass might increase. For where there is no Law, there is no transgression either. And how would anyone see the forgiveness of transgression and of the ease toward it, if the Law had not first condemned us? That what I say is true, and that the argument on this is not some faded or ugly thing, Paul will help, saying, 'So the Law was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom it has been promised, ordained through angels.' (Galatians 3:19) And being very wise, he tries to cut off in advance the inventions and questions that will sometimes be found by some. For it was likely that some would blame the delay of the righteousness in faith, and say that the coming-in of the Law in between became a setting-aside of that ancient promise. That is why he says, 'Is the Law then against the promises of God (Galatians 3:21)? Let it not be. For if a Law had been given that was able to make alive, righteousness would truly have been in Law. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Law was added after the promise and why that does not cancel the promise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The law was not given to nullify the blessings; it walled our nature around for a time, holding us back from sin, until we could be released to justification through faith.
comments.comment: It is not possible, then, nor even reasonable, to say that the law was given to nullify the blessings (Galatians 3:21). Since it was not from the beginning but later that God saw fit for us to enjoy justification by grace, Paul says, our nature was for a time being walled around by laws, hindered and held back from every activity of sin, so that, fit and ready, we might be released from the fortress of the law for the justification being opened up through faith (Galatians 3:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law came first and how it served until faith was revealed.
comments.author: Gennadius of Constantinople
comments.work: Fragments on the Letter to the Galatians

comments.capsule: The law gave knowledge of God, which prepared for grace.
comments.comment: Even if the law provided nothing else, but provided the knowing of God (Gal 3:23). And the knowing of God made ready for the reception of grace.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A tutor carries his pupils on to something greater, so the law leads us to Christ, and Paul counted its things as rubbish beside knowing him.
comments.comment: The Lord Himself is the light, and He “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22); He shows the true and glorified face of the law to the wise, who are sanctified in the Spirit and made radiant through faith in Christ. For the law leads us like a tutor to Christ (Galatians 3:24); and one appointed to lead others to someone else does not have his pupils stop at himself, but rather carries them on to something better and greater than himself. That is why the inspired Paul says that he counted the things in the law as rubbish “because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's picture of the law as a tutor.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law was brought in beforehand as a tutor to lead the people of old to Christ and show the truth through riddles, so the move to the truth makes its meaning clearer.
comments.comment: The law, then, was brought in beforehand to be a tutor for the people of old, leading them to the mystery of Christ (Galatians 3:24), and to give them glimpses of the truth through riddles. That is how we define Christ as the fulfilment of the law and the prophets, and quite rightly. Or would not the truth reasonably be understood to be the fulfilment of every obscure riddle? And how could anyone doubt it? So the passage from what was in shadows to the truth does not do away with the laws given through Moses; rather, it makes their meaning clearer.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is the beginning of bodily conduct, habituating the mind toward what is higher, and Christ is perfection.
comments.comment: Christ did not answer him [the man who asked] as he thought, but leads him up to the law — not because the law is perfection (“no one is justified in the law,” according to what is written), but because practice according to the law is a kind of entrance to eternal life, little by little habituating the mind of those being tutored toward what is higher. For “the law has become our tutor unto Christ.” (Galatians 3:24) So the law is the beginning of bodily conduct, and Christ is perfection; for the beginning of goods, he says, is to do what is just. The law shows the just; Christ shows the good.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Baptized believers have Christ as their garment, and he becomes everything to them: table, garment, house, head and root.
comments.comment: [To the newly baptized:] For you have the greatest garment, you have a spiritual table, you have the glory from above, and Christ becomes everything for you: table, garment, house, head, and root. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). See how he has become your garment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a vivid way what it means to put on Christ.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: God clothed Adam in a tunic, but the baptized put on Christ.
comments.comment: … In the paradise, after the transgression, God clothed Adam in tunics of skin. Let us see what he put on. That one there put on a tunic; here, 'as many as were baptized into Christ, have put on Christ' (Galatians 3:27).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Baptism, not keeping the law, clothes us with Christ and makes grace common to all.
comments.comment: Not the observance of the law, he says, makes those who believed better than the Gentiles than the Jews, but the power of baptism, providing to clothe oneself with Christ, makes the grace common to all together: barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male (Gal 3:27–28). And the female and the male were not merely mixed—insofar as one sought through the word toward what was set before him—but if baptism brings the male and the female differing into one grace, how much more the Greek and the Jew.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: In this life there are differences of small and great and slave, but in the coming age these fall away and only works show who is great and free.
comments.comment: … in this present life, a difference has been established between the small and the great and the slave, bringing greed into variety. But in the coming age, Paul says, 'there is neither male' 'nor female, there is neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28). Similarly he would say, as neither rich nor poor, but the demonstration of works, by which the one in this living will be considered great and free there, though small or a slave.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those called sons before Christ were like a child heir under guardians, and the fullness of time came with the sojourn of Jesus Christ, when people would receive adoption.
comments.comment: If, then, God is called Father, and those begotten by the word of faith in him are sons, yet the firm and unfallen character of sonship is not to be seen among the ancients. At any rate the very passages we set out show those called sons to be blameworthy — since, according to the Apostle, 'while the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a slave, though lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the term appointed by the father.' (Galatians 4:1) … But 'the fullness of time' lies in the sojourn of our Lord Jesus Christ, when those who will receive the adoption — as Paul teaches in these words: 'For you received not a spirit of slavery unto fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, wherein we cry: Abba, Father.' (Romans 8:15)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The elemental principles of the world were like guardians and stewards who tutor the immature toward what is beneficial.
comments.comment: Paul took the elemental principles of the world in the rank of guardians and stewards who tutor the immature in age toward what is beneficial—principles to which we were, because of our immature knowledge, beneficially enslaved (Galatians 4:3). He would not, I think, have taken sun and moon into the rank of guardians, because subjection to them would be unprofitable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by being enslaved under the elements, in plain terms.
comments.author: Gennadius of Constantinople
comments.work: Fragments on the Letter to the Galatians

comments.capsule: Christ was born of a woman from the earth, not brought down from heaven.
comments.comment: For Christ did not bring His own flesh down to us from above, out of heaven; rather, He was born according to the flesh of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who was herself one of those on the earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Human nature had to rise again by full obedience, and God sent his Son, born from a woman, to be found as a human on earth and obey the Father.
comments.comment: So since human nature was condemned by the sentence of death through the first-formed one’s disobedience, it had to rise again toward its original blamelessness by making a full showing of obedience. But this was already much and far beyond humanity’s measures … So the God and Father, summing up all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10)… “sent forth his Son, born from a woman,” (Galatians 4:4) so that taking a body like ours and making it his own, he might be found as a human on earth not knowing sin, and thus having become wholly obedient to God the Father, justify human nature in himself and free it from death’s bonds
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God sent his Son born of a woman: to give the obedience that Adam's disobedience lacked.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: He became under the law so as to become brother to those under it, and so we receive adoption.
comments.comment: “But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, become from a woman, become under law, so that he might buy out those under law, so that we might receive the adoption.” (Galatians 4:4–5) As God he became under law so that he might also become brother to those under law; for thus we have received the adoption (Galatians 4:5)
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why God's Son came under the law: so that we might receive adoption.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Since the Spirit of the Son, born of a woman and under law, is the Holy Spirit by whom we cry Abba, Father, that Son must be God.
comments.comment: So if he had not become under law and from a woman, we would not even be brothers to the Lord and God by nature; but since he became so, we have been enriched with what is his. The inspired Paul makes proof of the matter, bringing at once: “And because you are sons, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father.” (Galatians 4:6) How then is the Spirit of the one from a woman and under law the Holy Spirit, through whom we also cry Abba, Father, unless Christ is God, being one and Son?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Keeping the Sabbath, new moons and feasts after grace is serving otherwise, like worshipping the elements.
comments.comment: Now he wishes to show that after the grace has come, even if someone seems to keep the Sabbath, new moons, and feasts according to the law, just as if a Gentile, being a worshiper of idols, were worshipping the elemental things, he is serving otherwise (Gal 4:8–10).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Watching hours, days and seasons is unfitting for those known by God, since it gives to the world's elements an honor that God would have.
comments.comment:
Cyril: And what? Do you not say it is all-shameful and truly next-door to such evils—the watching days, and hours, and seasons, and years, and the waxing and waning of the lunar cycle?

Palladius: And very much. For most clearly the divine Paul makes the matter a charge for those having been saved from the nations, saying: ‘But then not knowing God, you were enslaved to those by nature not being gods; yet now having known God, or rather having been known by God, how do you turn again upon the weak and poor elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again from of old above? You observe days, and months, and years, and seasons; I fear you, lest somehow I have labored into you in vain.’ (Galatians 4:8-11)

Cyril: The watching of hours then and of days—and I would add also that of seasons—is altogether unfitting for those not having been ignorant of the one and by nature God, or rather for those having been known by him through faith, and having been called unto the intimacy through the grace; for he runs back backward, having let go the boast in Christ, the one having chosen to do this; and he has no longer saved his own mind free-loving, yet rather emptily runs under the yoke of the ancient wandering, distributing to the world’s elements an honor which God would have, and crowning with the highest glories the things having been called unto genesis by the nods of the one who has made. And elements of a world he calls the as-it-were portions of the all—seasons and months, and their measurements, being completed through hours and days (Galatians 4:8–11)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Those who know God are known by him, for when we know God he knows us.
comments.comment: The diligent are known by God; for the Lord knew those who were His, and they know Him. For the apostle says also to the Galatians: 'but once they did not know God, but now they know God, and even more so they are known by God' (Gal 4:9). When we know God, He knows us; for 'if anyone' 'is ignorant, he is unknown', clearly meaning that if anyone knows, he is known.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what Paul means by 'known by God'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Weak elements are not evil but cannot make people pious.
comments.comment: And regarding the weak elements, having said this, he did not accuse them of being evil, but of being unable to grow rich and pious.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A festival is doing what one ought, and the one who prays always and offers bloodless sacrifices in his prayers truly keeps festival, which is why Paul's words seem lofty.
comments.comment: For “a festival,” as one of the Greek wise men well says, “is nothing other than doing what one ought” (Thucydides 1.70). And he truly keeps festival who does “what he ought,” praying always (1 Thessalonians 5:17), and continually offering the bloodless sacrifices in his prayers to the divine. That is why Paul’s words seem to me most lofty: “Do you observe days and months and seasons and years? I fear for you, that I may somehow have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:10–11)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's change from rebuke to exhortation comes from the pain of his heart, since he writes from fatherly affection and for healing.
comments.comment: Do not think, he says, that I have some other kind of grief toward you and because of this I am rebuking you (Gal 4:12); for the passion of pain constantly forces the form of the word to change, now to rebuke and now to exhort, and sometimes to accuse and sometimes to lament. Therefore, here he teaches as what is written, that he writes through fatherly affection—for 'I have not been wronged by you,' he says—but also for healing
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul says he does not speak from envy, for it would have been better had they too been perfected by faith, and he wants the Galatians to be zealous ones all may imitate.
comments.comment: And since he said that those desire not you, but are zealous for you, so that they might have perfection for themselves by not keeping the law, but are zealous for you, he proceeded to say that I say these things not out of envy toward them; for it would have been better if they also had been perfected by using faith, and it would have been an unhindered thing for them to be zealous for and to imitate us. And you therefore do such things which make you become zealous ones, so that all may imitate you, and not when I come, being ashamed of you, you become such people, but even in my absence you correct yourselves.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The mind that shares in God becomes his image, as one who shares in virtue images it, and Paul urges that it be imaged according to Christ.
comments.comment: … it has been previously stated that the mind and the soul are man; this, participating in God through His communion, becomes His image, just as we say that the one participating in virtue images it, which even Paul, speaking in Christ, knows and exhorts to be imaged according to Christ: 'until Christ is formed in you' (Gal 4:19) … teaching that the thought concerning Christ, being a true soul approaching, characterizes and images it according to Him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being formed into Christ gives us the riches of the divine image, while he is that image by nature and in substance.
comments.comment: Through Him and in Him we have been sealed into the divine and spiritual image. For the divine apostle himself, writing to the Galatians, said, “My little children, for whom I am again in the pains of birth until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And if, by being formed into Christ, we gain the riches of the divine image in ourselves, then He Himself is the image of God the Father and His exact likeness, not as we are, called to likeness by sharing in holiness, but rather by nature and in substance.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Taking the old stories of wives and maidservants as figures is not our own teaching, and we are to imitate their spiritual meaning, not their bodily acts.
comments.comment: That brides and maidservants are to be taken in a figurative sense is not our own teaching; we have received it from wise men of old. One of them said, stirring his hearer to figurative interpretation: “Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, the son of the free woman through the promise. These things are spoken in allegory: for these women are two covenants, one from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar” (Galatians 4:21–24); and a little later: “But the Jerusalem above,” he says, “is free, which is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). Whoever cares to take up the Epistle to the Galatians will learn in what way the passages about the marriages and the unions with maidservants have been allegorised; for the word wishes us too to imitate not what are thought to be the bodily acts of those who did these things, but, as the apostles of Jesus are accustomed to call them, the spiritual ones.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls the story an allegory because it is true history that is also a prophecy made through deeds of what was to come.
comments.comment:
For allegory does not consist in spoken words, but introduces something else appearing from the sequence of the meanings according to the substance, such as 'Love me from the mouth of loves' in the Song of Songs; for there neither love nor hair nor belly nor thighs nor anything else is literally, but others are introduced through others, and this is the principal kind of allegory.

Here also the history is confessed, and it has been demonstrated that it is a type of what is to come. The prophecy through works is now called allegory. For of the prophecies, some are through words only, such as 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb,' others are through works only, such as Moses lifting up the serpent in the wilderness …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'allegory' means and why Paul can call the story of Abraham's sons an allegory.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The present Jerusalem is slave with her children, for slavery follows the promise of earthly things, while freedom comes from the citizenship in heaven.
comments.comment: In Galatians 4:25, he [Paul] did not simply refer to Mount Sinai, but also noted that the Ishmaelites' desert extends all the way to it. At Sinai the law was given for the slavery of offspring, and from Mount Sinai the tablets that were given were carried among Israel, and often having been moved from place to place, they were finally established in Jerusalem. Because of this he brought it forward; it corresponds to the present Jerusalem, which slaves alongside its children. Where there is the promise of land, and possession, and marriage, and human things, slavery follows; but where there is deliverance from earthly cares and from bonds, and in the heavens is the citizenship, from that citizenship comes freedom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul ties Sinai to slavery and the Jerusalem above to freedom.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A Christian's homeland is the free heavenly Jerusalem, his way of life is above, and his relatives are all the saints.
comments.comment: A Christian has no city on earth, but the heavenly Jerusalem. For the heavenly Jerusalem is free, and she is our mother (Galatians 4:26). A Christian has no earthly occupation, but fulfills the way of life above. For our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). A Christian has all the saints as relatives and fellow citizens. For we are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household (Ephesians 2:19)
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Gospel disciples should not carry a heavy yoke, since Christ calls his yoke good.
comments.comment: Similarly, Paul, speaking in Christ, writes to the Galatians, who wish to be circumcised sensually after the gospel: 'Stand fast, therefore, and do not be held again by a yoke of slavery' (Galatians 5:1). For it was no longer following to place the disciples of the gospel under oppression and the heavy yoke, having been persuaded by the one who said: 'My yoke is good' (Matthew 11:30)
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why Paul tells the Galatians to stand fast against a yoke of slavery.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Honoring the law's circumcision after the mystery of Christ cuts a person off from him, since the old commandment gave way to the new.
comments.comment: He [Paul] also rebuked others for honoring the circumcision of the law after the mystery of Christ. ‘You have been cut off from Christ,’ he says, ‘you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen from grace. But we, through faith, await the hope of righteousness’ (Galatians 5:4–5). He said too that the old commandment had been made useless, since it was not without fault, and that the other, that is, the commandment of the Gospel, had been brought in to take its place (Hebrews 7:18–19; Hebrews 8:7)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Being persuaded does not come from God, though the persuasive words do, for the hearer must choose and assent.
comments.comment: And that, even if the speaking of persuasive words comes from God, being persuaded at any rate does not come from God, Paul teaches clearly when he says: “This persuasion does not come from Him who calls you” (Galatians 5:8). Of the same kind too is the saying: “If you are willing and listen to Me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are not willing and do not listen to Me, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). For if someone is to will what the one who admonishes says, and, having listened to it, is to become worthy of God’s promises, there must be the hearer’s choice and his assent to what is said.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by saying that this persuasion is not from the one who calls.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's power weakens the flesh's impulses, so that those who walk by the Spirit do not carry out its desire.
comments.comment: Holy Scripture somewhere calls this [the uncleanness of the flesh's impulses] a law of sin dwelling in the members of the flesh, waging war against the law of the mind, and dragging us toward what is forbidden (Romans 7:23). But cut as with a razor by the power and working of the Holy Spirit, it grows weak, and even if it somehow springs up again in us, it is all the more quickly shorn away. For, ‘walk by the Spirit,’ he says, ‘and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh’ (Galatians 5:16)
comments.selected_reason: Shows how walking by the Spirit overcomes the desires of the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The law's memory of sin, and its allowing of eating, belonged to training the mind until one came who teaches not to walk according to the flesh.
comments.comment: In Galatians 5:17, he [Paul] asks why one who pulls away through the law remembers sin. Because the law commanded luxury, and because of this desire is divided and, being uncontainable toward sin, leads onward. For this reason, when there was a memory of the law, there was also a memory of sin. For in the letter to the Romans, mentioning the law, he also brought forward the correction through the Lord, for those living according to the flesh are unable to please God. And why was luxury and eating permitted? Because the abstention from the acknowledged evils would not have progressed, unless eating and drinking were given to them. For the lawgiver knew that it is impossible to restrain pleasures while living in luxury. Finally, he wished to discipline the mind, so that it might know what is good and what is bad and what is pious; for he foresaw that he who adds to what is lacking in the law was to come, I mean, not to walk according to the flesh, as Paul says.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Those of Christ crucified the flesh, so the gospel life is wholly given to God.
comments.comment: … the evangelical way of life does not have at all the being divided toward the things of flesh, or toward the affairs in the world, but wholly as it were consecrating to God those who have come under Christ. For ‘Those of Jesus Christ,’ (Galatians 5:24) he says, ‘have crucified the flesh with the passions and the desires.’
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The servant of Christ, crucified to the world, is held back from its works and boasts unceasingly.
comments.comment: 'May it never be to me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world' (Galatians 6:14). For the world having been crucified so that it no longer operates, being prevented from where it wishes to go and doing what it loves, the servant of Christ is crucified to it, so that even though his feet and hands are prevented from operating, he will unceasingly boast, declaring, 'I have been crucified with Christ.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for the world to be crucified to Paul and Paul to the world.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul boasts in Christ's cross because he knows the one who suffered in the flesh for us to be true God.
comments.comment: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” (Galatians 6:14) Blessed David sings, “I will boast in God my Savior.” (Habakkuk 3:18) The saying is wise and holy: we ought not to glory in a human being, but in God. How then does Paul say he boasts in the cross of Christ? He ought rather to do that in God. Yet the Spirit-bearer boasts in the death of Christ; so he knows him to be true God who suffered for us in the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Paul names a new creation, since one who lives in Christ is a citizen of heaven and not under the law.
comments.comment: In Galatians 6:14–15, so that it might not be thought that he [Paul] is making a substitute for circumcision, and giving a pretext of circumcision and condemnation to the opponents, he most beautifully brought forward the last thing, that neither circumcision avails nor uncircumcision, but he said a new creation. Concerning which elsewhere: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. If it is new, he says, a creation, let him not become under the law; for he who lives according to the law lives in the world, but he who lives in Christ is a citizen in the heavens. Therefore the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
